chunks: Muhammad ibn al-Hasan al-Saffar, from Ali ibn Muhammad al-Qassani, from al-Qasim ibn Muhammad, from Sulayman ibn Dawud al-Minqari, from Hafs ibn Ghiyath, who said:

I asked Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) about jihad: Is it a sunnah or an obligation? He said: 'Jihad is of four types: two are obligatory, one is sunnah and is not performed except with the obligation, and one is sunnah.'
As for one of the two obligations: it is the man's striving against his own self regarding the sins of Allah, and it is one of the greatest forms of jihad.
And the striving against 'those who are near you from the disbelievers' is an obligation.

As for the jihad that is sunnah and is not performed except with the obligation: the striving against the enemy is obligatory upon the entire community, and if they leave jihad, punishment will reach them, and this is from the punishment of the community.
And it is sunnah for the Imam alone to go to the enemy with the community and strive against them.
As for the jihad that is sunnah: whenever a man establishes a sunnah and strives in its establishment and attainment, then working and exerting oneself in it is among the best of deeds.

Because it is reviving a sunnah. The Prophet (peace be upon him and his family) said: 'Whoever establishes a good sunnah, he has its reward and the reward of those who act upon it until the Day of Judgment, without any of their rewards being diminished.'

key_terms.الْإِمَامُ: The Imam, specifically in the context of religious and political leadership
key_terms.الْجِهَادُ: Striving or exertion in the path of God

ai.seo_question: What are the four types of jihad according to Shia hadith?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) delineates jihad into four categories, distinguishing between the individual obligation of self-purification and the collective duty of defending against neighboring disbelievers, which incurs communal punishment if neglected. He further identifies the Imam’s specific leadership in battle as a sunnah performed alongside the community, while defining the third sunnah as the active propagation of prophetic traditions, linking it to the reward of 'sunnah hasanah.' This classification underscores the Shia scholarly view that jihad encompasses both military defense and spiritual-intellectual propagation, with the Imam playing a central role in the former.
